changes.reason: Checked against lines 1-3 under the reading the drafter asked about. Line 1 states the reason with because: there is nowhere to turn round. Line 2's two miles of sea wall describe his walk from the shelter. 'Nowhere to turn round' implies the way goes on but has no turning space, so the text does not make the sea wall the cause. To defend it, a child has to supply a cause the text never gives. 'Went on from there' makes a weaker causal claim than the stored 'begin there', so this is no more defensible than the value already signed. The within-span tag fits: true at line 2, answering what lies ahead rather than why the bus stops. The execution's line numbers are right: because and nowhere are on line 1, 'to turn round. From the shelter ... sea wall' on line 2. Breaks both overlap tells.

Wrong under every reading. Lines 14-15 make the offer his ('so I said I would get her a picture'), and no line has Nan ask; line 15-16's 'agrees with most things' is not a request. Cause-agent-swap names the mistake: the right event is given to the wrong character. Execution checked: the offer is at lines 14-15, the calendar at line 14. Breaks both overlap tells.

The step down into water and the piece of wall are at lines 8-9, at Saltmere (confirmed at lines 28-30). They are not in the mud below the wall in the window at lines 18-23, so the value is wrong scope under every reading. Execution checked: step and wall at lines 8-9; 'Below me a boat lay in the mud with its ribs showing' at line 20; gull at line 21. It takes the key's comma, the ', and' and the 11 words, so the comma, two-part and length tells all tie.

Line 36 is Nan's saying, not a real bell. Lines 37-39 give the buoy, and he decides that was what she meant. So 'a bell in the chapel' makes nothing, and the option fails on its first claim. The sea taking the place (lines 10-11) does not rescue it. Plausible-not-stated fits; the content is the same as the stored value. Execution checked: no chapel on the map at line 6, 'took the lot' at lines 10-11, buoy and knocking at line 37. Breaks the only-comma tell. Two options now have commas and two do not, so no reverse tell.

'Even then' at line 41 makes holding it in both hands something done in spite of the shake, never its cause. Reading it as 'is why' is exactly the relation-word flip the tag names, and no reading makes two hands the cause. Execution checked: both hands and 'even then the picture came out' on line 41; 'grey and shaken ... where my hand had moved' on line 42.

No line says the phone is faulty. Lines 40-42 give the failing light and his moving hand. Plausible-not-stated is unchanged and fits. Execution checked: the light going is at line 40 and the hand moving at line 42. Adding 'not' means the key is no longer the only option with not.

Lines 27-28 say he 'didn't half a quarter like the job till I had this talk', with 'but there's my hand on it now'. So liking it before the talk drops the didn't, as the negation-dropped tag says. I tested the modern British 'didn't half' (meaning 'very much') reading. It cannot stand with 'but there's my hand on it now' and Silver's praise at line 29. The stored 'from the very start' carried the same exposure, so nothing new is defensible. Execution quotes lines 27-28 correctly. It ties the key at 10 words.

An expression of horror is on her face, not in the wardrobe, so it cannot answer what she finds. The within-span retag is right: it is true at line 9 and answers how she looks. The row's hintCore ('One of these gives her feeling instead of the thing') still points at this seat. Execution checked: the expression is at line 9, and 'at the bottom but a heap of rolls' is at line 12. Small note: 'returned' is on line 8, but the quoted phrase is on line 9. Breaks both overlap tells.

Lines 21-25 have her sob only about grandmother's bread. Home appears only in Clara's words at line 29, and the mountain appears nowhere, so the value is wrong under every reading. Plausible-not-stated fits. Execution checked: 'sobbing out' at line 23, 'all for grandmother' at lines 23-24. Note: 'back ... again' is mildly redundant. It puts this distractor one word past the key (a flip, not a tie), but that points away from the key.

Clara's reason at line 29 is 'would have been hard and stale by then' (when you go home). The row's walkScript says outright that they are not stale yet. 'Hard and stale by now' is a reason Clara does not give, so it is wrong under every reading. Minimal-pair-skim names it: the same words with one detail, then for now. The cupboard is true (lines 11 and 14). Execution checked: 'when you go home; yours would have been hard and stale by then' is all on line 29. Breaks the length and overlap tells. At 13 words to the key's 11 it flips rather than ties, which is not a giveaway.

Lines 33-36 give her wish to depend on the promise. She is in despair and weeping (lines 21-25), but no line gives anger. Anger is an adjacent emotion, as emotion-label-approximation names. 'Her bread was taken away' is true (lines 14 and 24), so only the anger is wrong. Execution checked: 'to make sure that she could depend upon it' at line 33; the promise is at line 32. It ties the key at 11 words.

The value is sound. Line 44 is unambiguous ('after wrapping a handkerchief round it, she stuck it'), so cupboard-then-handkerchief is wrong under every reading. The fault is the TAG. In entries, en-chronology-collapse is 'picks a cause that happens LATER in the passage than the effect being asked about'. 'What does Heidi do with the hat?' asks about no cause and no effect. The execution's closing words ('only the order rules it out') borrow that tag's description, which is a story fitted to the tag. The mistake here is a match on gist that differs from the text in one detail, the order: that is en-minimal-pair-skim, as the drafter's own note says. Re-propose with tag en-minimal-pair-skim; the value and execution facts can stand (line 44 wrap and stuck, line 45 as far back as she could).

Tested as the drafter asked. The second half is true: line 55 says 'his hand shook so that it jumped under mine'. The first claim, illness, is stated nowhere. The only explanation in the window is line 54's 'as a man looks who thinks on flight', which is fear. Earlier, at lines 33-34, he went pale on seeing the King. A child who reads the signs as illness has ignored the one line that interprets them, so this is not a second answer. The brief allows 'the first claim is the wrong one', and the content matches the signed stored value. Plausible-not-stated names it. en-physical-vs-emotional-cue would be the sharper tag if it is ever retagged. Execution checked: looked right and left at lines 53-54, thinks on flight at line 54, hand shook at line 55. It ties the comma, two-part and word-length tells.

Having danced at Topham's house (lines 66-67) is why he might be recognised: the danger, not the relief. Lines 67-68 give the relief, blind as a bat and no claim of acquaintance. Within-span fits. Execution checked: Grosvenor Square and 'danced a score of' at line 66, 'times' and 'as blind as a bat' at line 67. Breaks the whole-passage overlap tell.

'In and out' is true (lines 6-7). The claim that fails is 'she cannot count them'. Line 7 gives the count (two in, one out), and lines 7-8 say her eyes do the counting without being asked. The passage states the contrary, so contradicted-by-the-text fits, and no reading lets her be unable to count. Execution's line numbers checked. Breaks the length tell.

Line 11 is his next action at the bolt. Line 10 ('Your mum says a lot of things on her way out of the door') is what he does with her words. I tested whether 'looks at the door' could be read as ignoring her. It describes his attention to the bolt, and the row's hint ('Does he take it seriously?') sends the child to line 10, so it is not a second answer. Within-span fits. Execution checked: the whole clause is on line 11, and the brush-off is on line 10.

No line has anyone show her anything. She found them herself (line 13) after her ball went down the side of the shed (lines 13-14), and line 21 says she told nobody. Plausible-not-stated fits. Execution checked. It ties the key at 10 words.

This seat replaces a stem-restating distractor, but the new value can also be ruled out from the stem alone. 'Two STILL go in ... as regular as buses' says the traffic has NOT changed. The question is 'How has the traffic under the boards changed?', and line 34 says it 'has changed'. So a child can drop it without reading lines 6-7, which is the same defect as the value it replaces. With 'Priya is looking past his shoulder' also falling to the stem (it is about Priya, not traffic), the row becomes two-from-four on the question alone. Fix: drop 'still' ('Two go in, and one comes out, as regular as buses.'). That is a true wrong-scope reading of line 7 that a child has to read to rule out, and it keeps the comma and two-part tie. As written, the execution's 'True at lines 6 and 7' is also not true of the word 'still'.

Line 39 is how often and how she has said it. What happens both times is at lines 39-40 (he answered a different question). The verbatim lure is a real within-span mistake, and the row's hint ('A count is not what she notices') targets it. Execution checked: everything quoted is on line 39, the answer runs from line 39 into line 40. Note: 11 words to the key's 8 overshoots a tie, but it points away from the key.
